summary: This unit covers where the coronary arteries arise, how they branch, which part of the heart each one feeds, and how the heart's veins drain back to the right atrium. The exam uses it to link a blocked artery to the wall that dies, the ECG leads that change, and the complications that follow.

points: Right coronary artery (RCA) arises from the right aortic sinus; left coronary artery (LCA) from the left aortic sinus.
Left main runs between the pulmonary trunk and left auricle, then splits into the LAD and the circumflex (LCx).
LAD (anterior interventricular artery) runs down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex.
LAD feeds the anterior LV wall, the apex, and the anterior two-thirds of the septum (septal perforators); diagonal branches feed the anterolateral wall.
LCx runs in the left atrioventricular (coronary) groove to the back; obtuse marginal branches feed the lateral LV wall.
RCA runs in the right atrioventricular groove.
Right (acute) marginal branch feeds the right ventricle.
SA nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 60% of hearts and from the LCx in about 40%.
AV nodal artery comes from the RCA in about 80% of hearts.
In a right-dominant heart the RCA gives the posterior descending artery (PDA), which feeds the posterior one-third of the septum and the inferior LV wall.
Dominance is defined by which artery gives the PDA.
Most hearts are right dominant (estimates run from about 67% to 85%); the rest are left dominant (PDA from LCx) or codominant.
Anterolateral papillary muscle has a double supply (LAD and LCx).
Posteromedial papillary muscle depends on the PDA alone, so it is the one that ruptures after an inferior MI.
Coronary sinus lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium.
Great cardiac vein runs with the LAD, middle cardiac vein with the PDA, small cardiac vein with the right marginal artery; all three reach the coronary sinus.
Anterior cardiac veins drain the front of the RV straight into the right atrium.
Smallest cardiac veins (venae cordis minimae) open directly into the chambers.
Resting coronary flow is about 225 mL/min, about 4 to 5% of cardiac output.
LV muscle is perfused mostly in diastole, because systole squeezes the intramyocardial vessels shut.
Tachycardia shortens diastole, so it cuts LV perfusion while raising demand.
The heart extracts about 70% of arterial oxygen at rest, so more demand must be met by more flow.
Adenosine and other local metabolites are the main coronary vasodilators.
The subendocardium has the highest wall stress and the least flow reserve, so it becomes ischemic first.

charts.title: Coronary arteries and their territories
rows: Anterior interventricular groove to the apex
Anterior LV wall, apex, anterior two-thirds of septum
Left atrioventricular groove to the posterior heart
Lateral and posterolateral LV wall, left atrium
Right atrium, most of the RV, SA node (about 60%), AV node (about 80%)
II, III, aVF (inferior), often with bradycardia or AV block
Posterior one-third of septum, inferior LV wall, posteromedial papillary muscle

tricks.label: Who gives the PDA wins
tricks.text: To name the dominant artery, ask only one question: which artery gives the posterior descending artery? Size of the vessel does not matter.

tricks.label: Veins shadow arteries
tricks.text: Pair each vein with its artery: great with LAD, middle with PDA, small with right marginal. All three empty into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

tricks.label: Diastole feeds the left
tricks.text: Anything that shortens diastole (fast heart rate) or lowers aortic diastolic pressure (aortic regurgitation, hypotension) starves the LV subendocardium first.

highYield: LAD is the most commonly occluded coronary artery, followed by the RCA, then the LCx.
Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) usually means RCA occlusion and can come with bradycardia or AV block.
Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture after inferior MI causes sudden acute mitral regurgitation.
Coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure.
Coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium.
Adenosine is the classic local metabolite that dilates coronary arterioles when demand rises.
pitfalls: Dominance is about who supplies the PDA; a large LCx can still sit in a right-dominant heart.
The SA node is usually fed by the RCA (about 60%), but in about 40% it comes from the LCx, so an LCx lesion can still cause sinus node problems.
The anterolateral papillary muscle rarely ruptures because it has two arteries; the posteromedial one has only the PDA.
Anterior cardiac veins and smallest cardiac veins bypass the coronary sinus, so the coronary sinus does not carry all cardiac venous blood.

dumps.p: Draw the heart from the front and from below. Label the left main, LAD, diagonal branch, circumflex, obtuse marginal, RCA, right marginal, and PDA. Shade and name the wall each artery feeds.

Left main splits into LAD and circumflex
LAD in the anterior interventricular groove reaching the apex
LAD territory: anterior LV wall, apex, anterior two-thirds of septum
Circumflex in the left atrioventricular groove feeding the lateral wall
RCA in the right atrioventricular groove with the right marginal branch to the RV
PDA in the posterior interventricular groove feeding the inferior wall and posterior one-third of septum
Note that the PDA source defines dominance

dumps.p: Trace a red cell from the aorta through the LAD, across the anterior wall capillaries, and back to the right atrium. Name each vessel and say when in the cardiac cycle the flow is highest.
l: Left aortic sinus to the left main coronary artery
Left main to LAD, then septal or diagonal branches
Capillaries of the anterior LV wall
Great cardiac vein running back up beside the LAD
Coronary sinus in the posterior atrioventricular groove
Opening into the right atrium
LV flow is highest in diastole because systole compresses intramyocardial vessels
About 70% of the oxygen is extracted on the way through

summary: This unit covers how arterial blood reaches the head, limbs, and abdominal organs, how venous blood returns, and how the portal system connects the gut to the liver. Exam questions name a vessel or a vertebral level and ask what it supplies, or describe a blockage and ask what tissue suffers.

points: Arch branches, right to left: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Brachiocephalic trunk splits into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
Common carotid divides at about the level of C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage) into internal and external carotids.
Descending thoracic aorta gives posterior intercostal, bronchial, and esophageal branches.
Enters the abdomen through the aortic hiatus at T12 and bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at L4.
Unpaired gut arteries: celiac trunk (T12), superior mesenteric artery (L1), inferior mesenteric artery (L3).
Paired branches: inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal (about L1), gonadal (about L2), and four pairs of lumbar arteries.
Celiac trunk gives the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.
Splenic flexure sits between SMA and IMA territories, a watershed zone for ischemic colitis.
Brain gets anterior flow from the internal carotids and posterior flow from the vertebral arteries (branches of the subclavians), which join as the basilar artery.
Circle of Willis links them: anterior communicating, anterior cerebral, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
Upper limb: subclavian becomes axillary at the lateral border of the first rib, then brachial at the lower border of teres major; brachial splits into radial and ulnar in the cubital fossa.

Lower limb: external iliac becomes femoral under the inguinal ligament, then popliteal at the adductor hiatus; popliteal splits into anterior tibial and the tibiofibular trunk (posterior tibial and fibular).
Dorsalis pedis is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery.
SVC forms from the two brachiocephalic veins; IVC forms from the common iliac veins at about L5.
Left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta just below the SMA; the left gonadal vein drains into it, while the right gonadal vein drains straight into the IVC.
Hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; the inferior mesenteric vein usually joins the splenic vein.
Portal blood passes through liver sinusoids, then leaves by the hepatic veins into the IVC.

notes.h: Where cardiac output goes at rest
points: Liver and gut together receive about a quarter of resting cardiac output, kidneys about a fifth.
Skeletal muscle gets about 15% at rest and the brain about 14%.
Heart muscle gets about 4 to 5% but uses oxygen at a very high rate.

charts.title: Abdominal aorta landmarks
rows: Foregut: stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, part of the pancreas, spleen
Midgut: distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon
Hindgut: distal one-third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal

rows: Esophageal veins draining to the azygos system

tricks.label: ABC'S
tricks.text: Aortic arch gives the Brachiocephalic trunk, left common Carotid, and left Subclavian, in that order from right to left.

tricks.label: Bifourcation
tricks.text: The abdominal aorta bifurcates at L4: bi-FOUR-cation.

tricks.label: One artery per gut segment
tricks.text: Foregut goes with the celiac trunk, midgut with the SMA, hindgut with the IMA. Find which segment the organ came from and you have its artery.

highYield: Celiac T12, SMA L1, renal about L1, gonadal about L2, IMA L3, bifurcation L4.
Left renal vein can be squeezed between the SMA and aorta (nutcracker phenomenon).
Left varicocele is more common because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.
Splenic flexure is a watershed area between SMA and IMA territories.
Portal hypertension opens anastomoses at the esophagus, umbilicus, and rectum.
The vertebral arteries come off the subclavians and join to form the basilar artery.
pitfalls: The spleen develops from mesoderm, yet it is supplied by the celiac trunk (splenic artery).
The pancreatic head has a double supply: superior pancreaticoduodenal (celiac) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (SMA) arteries.
The popliteal artery starts at the adductor hiatus, while the femoral artery starts at the inguinal ligament; mixing these up shifts the level of a lesion.
The right gonadal vein drains into the IVC; only the left one drains into the renal vein.

IMA at L3 supplying the hindgut

Left renal vein crossing anterior to the aorta below the SMA

summary: This unit covers how lymph is formed, how it moves, where it drains, and how lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, and mucosal lymphoid tissue are built. The exam asks about drainage routes, the zones of each lymphoid organ, and what goes wrong when lymph flow is blocked.

points: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended tubes with overlapping endothelial cells that act as one-way flap valves.
Anchoring filaments hold them open when the tissue swells.
They return filtered fluid and leaked plasma protein to the blood, about 2 to 3 L per day.
Lacteals in intestinal villi take up dietary fat as chylomicrons, which makes lymph milky (chyle).
Collecting lymphatics have valves and smooth muscle that contract in segments (lymphangions).
Skeletal muscle contraction, breathing, nearby arterial pulsation, and outside compression all push lymph forward.
A rise in interstitial fluid pressure increases lymph flow, up to a maximum.
Thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli (about L1 to L2), passes through the aortic hiatus, and drains into the left venous angle (left internal jugular and left subclavian junction).
Thoracic duct drains everything except the right upper body.
Right lymphatic duct (or its trunks separately) drains the right head, neck, arm, and right side of the thorax into the right venous angle.
Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow (B cells mature) and thymus (T cells mature).
Secondary lymphoid organs: lymph nodes, spleen, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer patches in the ileum, appendix).
Lymph node path: afferent vessels, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinuses, medullary sinuses, efferent vessel at the hilum.
Spleen filters blood: red pulp removes old red cells; white pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.
Thymus comes from the third pharyngeal pouch; positive selection happens in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla.
Lymphedema is protein-rich edema that becomes firm and nonpitting as fibrosis sets in.
Causes include lymph node removal or radiation (such as after breast cancer surgery), tumor, and filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti).
Thoracic duct injury leaks chyle into the pleural space (chylothorax).

charts.title: Zones of lymphoid organs
rows: B cells; germinal centers in secondary follicles
T cells and dendritic cells; high endothelial venules
T-cell activation; entry point for circulating lymphocytes
Plasma cells and macrophages in medullary cords
Antibody secretion and filtering of lymph
Removes old or damaged red cells
Immature T cells and cortical epithelial cells

charts.title: First lymph node group by region
rows: Scrotum, vulva, anal canal below the pectinate line, most of the superficial lower limb

tricks.label: Right upper corner
tricks.text: Only the right upper corner of the body (right head, neck, arm, and chest) goes to the right lymphatic duct. Every other region drains to the thoracic duct.

tricks.label: SHiNE SKiS
tricks.text: Encapsulated organisms that threaten people without a spleen: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis, Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Klebsiella pneumoniae, group B Streptococcus.

tricks.label: Cortex positive, medulla negative
tricks.text: In the thymus, the cortex keeps T cells that can bind self MHC (positive selection), and the medulla deletes T cells that bind self antigen too strongly (negative selection).

highYield: Testes drain to para-aortic nodes, while the scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
Paracortex is underdeveloped in DiGeorge syndrome because T cells are lacking.
Asplenia raises the risk of sepsis from encapsulated bacteria; Howell-Jolly bodies appear on the smear.
Thoracic duct empties into the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins.
Lymphedema fluid is protein rich, which drives fibrosis and nonpitting swelling.
Peyer patches sit in the ileum and contain M cells that sample gut antigens.
pitfalls: Anal canal below the pectinate line drains to superficial inguinal nodes; above it drains to internal iliac nodes.
Lymph node B cells sit in the cortex follicles, while T cells sit in the paracortex; in the spleen T cells sit in the periarteriolar sheath.
Lymphedema and cardiac edema both swell the legs, but lymphedema is protein rich and becomes nonpitting, while early edema from high venous pressure pits easily.
Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs; the spleen is secondary.

dumps.p: Draw a lymph node in cross section. Label where lymph enters and leaves, every sinus it passes through, and the B-cell, T-cell, and plasma-cell zones.
l: Afferent lymphatic vessels entering the convex surface
Capsule and subcapsular sinus
Cortex with primary and secondary follicles and germinal centers (B cells)
Paracortex with T cells and high endothelial venules
Medullary cords with plasma cells and macrophages
Medullary sinuses leading to the hilum
Efferent lymphatic vessel, artery, and vein at the hilum

dumps.t: Trace lymph back to the blood
dumps.p: Trace a drop of interstitial fluid from the left foot back into the blood. Then do the same for a drop from the right hand. Name each vessel and node group.
l: Lymphatic capillary with overlapping endothelial flaps
Collecting vessels with valves
Left foot: superficial inguinal nodes, then deep inguinal, external iliac, common iliac, and lumbar nodes
Lumbar trunks to the cisterna chyli near L1 to L2
Thoracic duct through the aortic hiatus to the left venous angle
Right hand: axillary nodes, then the subclavian trunk
Right lymphatic duct (or the trunks directly) to the right venous angle

summary: This unit covers the physics of blood flow (pressure, resistance, viscosity, turbulence), the Starling forces that move fluid across capillaries, and how tissues control their own flow. Board questions ask you to predict what happens to flow or pressure when one variable changes.

points: Flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance (Q = ΔP / R).
For the whole circulation, mean arterial pressure is about cardiac output times total peripheral resistance.
Poiseuille: resistance = 8ηL / (πr⁴), so radius matters most.
Halving the radius raises resistance 16 times and cuts flow to one-sixteenth at the same pressure.
Resistances in series add; in parallel, 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + and so on, so the total is lower than any single branch.
Organs sit in parallel, which lets each one change its own flow without changing the others much.
Velocity = flow divided by total cross-sectional area, so blood moves slowest in capillaries.
Hematocrit is the main determinant of viscosity; polycythemia raises viscosity and resistance, anemia lowers them.
Turbulence becomes more likely with high velocity, low viscosity, large diameter, and rough or narrowed vessels (Reynolds number).
Turbulence makes bruits and murmurs, such as flow murmurs in anemia.
Pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic; it widens with stiff arteries or a larger stroke volume.
MAP is about diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure at resting heart rates.
Veins are about 24 times more compliant than their matching arteries and hold about 64% of blood volume.
Law of Laplace: wall tension rises with pressure and radius, so a dilated ventricle or aneurysm faces more wall stress.
Starling: net filtration = Kf × [(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)].
Edema comes from higher capillary pressure, lower plasma oncotic pressure, leakier capillaries, or blocked lymphatics.
Lymph returns the small net filtrate and leaked protein to the blood.
Venous return is helped by venous valves, the skeletal muscle pump, and the drop in thoracic pressure during inspiration.
Metabolic control: adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, lactate, and low O₂ dilate arterioles in active tissue.
Myogenic control: stretch of arteriolar smooth muscle triggers contraction, which keeps flow steady when pressure rises (autoregulation).
Endothelium releases nitric oxide (from shear stress) and prostacyclin to dilate, and endothelin to constrict.
Sympathetic nerves constrict most arterioles through α1 receptors.
Constrictors in blood: norepinephrine, angiotensin II, vasopressin. Dilators: bradykinin, histamine, ANP, nitric oxide.
Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) report pressure to the nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla.

charts.title: Vessel segments
rows: Largest share of resistance and the biggest pressure drop
Set total peripheral resistance and divide flow among organs
Largest total cross-sectional area, slowest velocity
Most compliant, hold about 64% of blood volume
Blood reservoir; venoconstriction raises venous return

charts.title: Main control of flow by organ
rows: Local metabolites (adenosine, NO, CO₂) and low O₂
Local metabolites during exercise; sympathetic tone at rest

charts.title: Starling forces
rows: Rises in heart failure, venous obstruction, volume overload
Falls in nephrotic syndrome, liver failure, malnutrition
Into the capillary when positive (it is slightly negative in most loose tissues, which favors filtration)
Rarely a primary cause; it rises as edema builds and opposes further filtration
Rises with leaky capillaries (burns, inflammation) or lymphatic blockage

tricks.label: Blood follows Ohm's law
tricks.text: ΔP = Q × R works like V = I × R. Pressure is voltage, flow is current, and resistance is resistance. MAP = CO × TPR is the same idea for the whole body.

tricks.label: Radius to the fourth
tricks.text: When a question changes vessel radius, think in powers of two: half the radius gives 16 times the resistance; double the radius gives one-sixteenth.

tricks.label: Four ways to edema
tricks.text: Push harder (high Pc), pull weaker (low πc), leak more (high Kf or πi), or drain less (lymph block). Sort any edema cause into one of the four.

highYield: Arterioles are the main resistance vessels and the main site of blood pressure control.
Capillaries have the greatest total cross-sectional area and the slowest velocity.
Radius is raised to the fourth power in Poiseuille's law, so small changes in caliber cause large changes in flow.
Cerebral flow tracks PCO₂: hyperventilation lowers PCO₂ and constricts cerebral vessels.
Hypoxia dilates systemic vessels but constricts pulmonary vessels.
Nephrotic syndrome causes edema by lowering plasma oncotic pressure.
Isolated systolic hypertension in older adults reflects stiff, less compliant arteries.
pitfalls: Adding a parallel vascular bed lowers total resistance; adding a segment in series raises it.
Blood velocity is lowest in capillaries even though each capillary is tiny, because their combined area is the largest.
Pulmonary vessels constrict to hypoxia, the opposite of systemic vessels.
Higher hematocrit raises viscosity and resistance; anemia lowers them and favors turbulence.

dumps.p: Draw three stacked line graphs across the aorta, arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins, and vena cava: one for pressure, one for total cross-sectional area, one for velocity. Explain each shape.
l: Pressure is highest in the aorta and pulsatile in large arteries
Steepest pressure drop across the arterioles
Pulsatility is mostly gone by the capillaries
Venous pressure is low and near zero at the right atrium
Cross-sectional area peaks at the capillaries
Velocity is the mirror image of area, lowest in capillaries
Velocity rises again as veins merge into the vena cava

dumps.p: Build a table on blank paper of the four Starling forces. For each, write which way it pushes fluid and one disease that changes it to cause edema. Add the role of lymph.
l: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out
Plasma oncotic pressure pulls fluid in
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration when positive
Interstitial oncotic pressure pulls fluid out
Heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure
Nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis lowers plasma oncotic pressure
Burns or inflammation raise permeability
Lymph removes the net filtrate; blockage causes lymphedema

summary: This unit covers how the heart and vessels respond during a single bout of exercise and how they adapt with regular training. Questions ask you to predict changes in heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure, and resistance, and to tell an athlete's heart from disease.

points: Central command from the motor cortex and reflexes from muscle mechanoreceptors and metaboreceptors raise sympathetic output.
The early rise in heart rate comes from vagal withdrawal; sympathetic drive takes over as intensity rises.
Venoconstriction, the skeletal muscle pump, and deeper breathing push more blood back to the heart.
Heart rate rises roughly in step with workload.
Stroke volume rises from more filling (Frank-Starling) and stronger contraction; in many untrained people it levels off at moderate intensity.
Cardiac output can rise about four- to fivefold in hard exercise in untrained adults, and more in trained endurance athletes.
Oxygen uptake follows the Fick principle: VO₂ = cardiac output × arteriovenous O₂ difference.
The arteriovenous O₂ difference widens because active muscle extracts more oxygen.
Active muscle arterioles dilate to local metabolites (K⁺, adenosine, H⁺, CO₂, lactate) and nitric oxide.
Muscle blood flow can rise up to about 25 times in strenuous exercise.
Sympathetic constriction cuts flow to the gut, kidneys, and inactive muscle.
Skin flow rises as body temperature climbs, to shed heat.
Brain flow stays fairly constant; coronary flow rises with cardiac work.

notes.h: Blood pressure in two kinds of exercise
points: Dynamic (aerobic) exercise: systolic pressure rises, diastolic stays about the same or falls slightly, total peripheral resistance falls.
Static (isometric) exercise: contracting muscle squeezes its own vessels, so systolic and diastolic pressure both rise sharply.
Dynamic exercise is mainly a volume load on the heart; static exercise is mainly a pressure load.
Endurance training enlarges the LV cavity with proportional wall thickening (eccentric remodeling), so stroke volume rises.
Plasma and blood volume increase, which raises preload.
Resting heart rate falls, mostly from higher vagal tone; maximum heart rate changes little.
Maximal cardiac output and VO₂max rise.
Trained muscle has more capillaries and mitochondria, so it extracts more oxygen.
Regular exercise lowers resting blood pressure, raises HDL, lowers triglycerides, and improves insulin sensitivity and endothelial nitric oxide release.

charts.title: Acute response: dynamic vs static exercise
Athlete's heart vs hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
rows: After a period of rest from training

tricks.label: Fick for exercise
tricks.text: VO₂ = CO × (arterial minus venous O₂ content). Exercise raises both terms: the heart pumps more, and muscle pulls more oxygen out of each liter.

tricks.label: Run vs lift
tricks.text: Running opens muscle vessels, so resistance falls and diastolic pressure holds steady. Lifting squeezes them shut, so both systolic and diastolic pressure climb.

tricks.label: Big tank, slow pump
tricks.text: The trained heart has a bigger LV and more blood volume, so each beat moves more blood and the resting rate can be lower for the same output.

highYield: In dynamic exercise total peripheral resistance falls because active muscle beds dilate.
Diastolic pressure stays about the same or falls slightly in dynamic exercise; it rises in static exercise.
Resting bradycardia in trained athletes is mainly from increased vagal tone.
The arteriovenous O₂ difference widens during exercise and after training.
Exercise shunts blood away from the gut and kidneys toward muscle, heart, and skin.
Athlete's heart regresses after training stops; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not.
pitfalls: Cardiac output at rest stays about the same after training; the lower heart rate is balanced by a larger stroke volume.
Maximum heart rate does not rise with training; the gains in maximal output come from stroke volume.
A rise in systolic pressure during running is normal; a fall in systolic pressure as workload increases is abnormal.
Brain blood flow stays fairly constant in exercise even though cardiac output rises several-fold.

dumps.p: Build a table with two columns, rest and hard dynamic exercise. Fill in what happens to heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, systolic pressure, diastolic pressure, total peripheral resistance, arteriovenous O₂ difference, muscle flow, and gut and kidney flow.

Stroke volume up
Cardiac output up about four- to fivefold (more in trained athletes)
Systolic pressure up
Diastolic pressure about the same or slightly down
Total peripheral resistance down
Arteriovenous O₂ difference wider
Muscle flow up as much as about 25 times
Gut and kidney flow down from sympathetic constriction

dumps.t: Trace the reflexes of a run
dumps.p: Trace the steps from the moment someone starts running to the rise in cardiac output. Include the nerve signals, the heart, the veins, and the muscle arterioles.
l: Central command from the motor cortex
Muscle mechanoreceptor and metaboreceptor input
Medullary cardiovascular centers respond
Vagal withdrawal raises heart rate first
Sympathetic drive raises heart rate and contractility
Venoconstriction and the muscle pump raise venous return
More filling raises stroke volume (Frank-Starling)

summary: This unit covers how lipids travel in the blood, how the heart makes its ATP, and which vitamins, minerals, and cofactors the heart and vessels depend on. The exam links a biochemical defect or deficiency to a heart or vessel problem, such as thiamine and high-output failure or homocysteine and thrombosis.

points: Exogenous path: intestine packs dietary triglyceride into chylomicrons (apo B-48), which reach the blood through lymph.
Lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium, activated by apo C-II, frees fatty acids from chylomicrons and VLDL.
Endogenous path: liver makes VLDL (apo B-100), which becomes IDL and then LDL as triglyceride is removed.
LDL delivers cholesterol to cells through the LDL receptor, which binds apo B-100.
HDL (apo A-I) carries cholesterol back to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport); apo A-I activates LCAT, which esterifies cholesterol.
CETP moves cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL, IDL, and LDL in exchange for triglyceride.
HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
LDL that enters the intima can be oxidized; macrophages take it up through scavenger receptors that are not downregulated, becoming foam cells.
Lipoprotein(a) is an LDL-like particle with apo(a), which resembles plasminogen; its level is mostly genetic and it adds atherosclerotic risk.
Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL; omega-3 fatty acids (EPA, DHA) lower triglycerides at higher intakes.
The adult heart at rest makes most of its ATP (roughly 60 to 90%) from fatty acid beta-oxidation; glucose, lactate, and ketones supply the rest.
Mitochondria fill about a third of cardiomyocyte volume, so the heart depends on a steady O₂ supply.
Long-chain fatty acids need carnitine and carnitine palmitoyltransferase I to enter mitochondria; malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I.
Creatine kinase moves high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to myofibrils as creatine phosphate.
In ischemia the heart switches to anaerobic glycolysis, lactate builds up, and contraction fails within a minute or two.
Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) carries electrons in the respiratory chain and is made from the same mevalonate pathway that statins block.
Thiamine (B1), as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase, and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase.
Thiamine deficiency with heart failure (wet beriberi) is a high-output state with dilated heart and peripheral vasodilation; risk is high in alcohol use disorder and malnutrition.
Homocysteine is remethylated to methionine by methionine synthase (needs B12 and folate) or converted to cystathionine by cystathionine beta-synthase (needs B6).
Deficiency of B12, folate, or B6 raises homocysteine, which injures endothelium and favors thrombosis.
Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen; scurvy causes fragile vessels, bleeding gums, and perifollicular hemorrhage.
Vitamin K is needed to gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S.
Potassium (normal about 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L) sets resting membrane potential; both low and high levels cause arrhythmias.
Calcium (normal about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL) triggers contraction through L-type channels and calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Magnesium is needed for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity; low magnesium increases renal potassium loss, so hypokalemia is hard to correct, and causes hypocalcemia by impairing PTH release and action.
Iron deficiency anemia causes a high-output, tachycardic state; iron overload (hemochromatosis) causes cardiomyopathy and conduction problems.
Selenium deficiency causes Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy.
Copper is a cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen and elastin; deficiency (as in Menkes disease) weakens arteries.

tricks.label: Thiamine has four enzymes
tricks.text: List them as pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase. All energy production slows without B1, and the heart fails in a high-output pattern.

tricks.label: MMA splits B12 from folate
tricks.text: Both deficiencies raise homocysteine. Only B12 deficiency also raises methylmalonic acid.

tricks.label: Apo letters by job
tricks.text: C-II cuts (activates lipoprotein lipase), E is the entry ticket to the liver for remnants, B-100 docks on the LDL receptor, A-I activates LCAT.

highYield: Wet beriberi: thiamine deficiency causing high-output heart failure.
Apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase; apo B-100 binds the LDL receptor.
Oxidized LDL taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors forms foam cells.
The resting adult heart burns mostly fatty acids for ATP.
Hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypokalemia and raises the risk of torsades de pointes.
Hyperkalemia shows peaked T waves; hypokalemia shows U waves.
Selenium deficiency causes Keshan cardiomyopathy.
Homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) causes arterial and venous thrombosis.
pitfalls: LDL receptors on cells are downregulated when cells have enough cholesterol; scavenger receptors on macrophages are not, which is why foam cells overfill.
Lowering homocysteine with B vitamins has not clearly reduced heart attacks in trials, so treat high homocysteine as a marker of risk and a sign of vitamin status.
Thiamine deficiency heart failure is high output with low resistance, unlike the low-output failure of most cardiomyopathies.
Hypocalcemia lengthens QT and hypercalcemia shortens it; potassium changes show up mostly in T and U waves.

summary: This unit covers single-gene and chromosomal disorders that affect the heart and vessels, plus the gene-expression and cell-cycle ideas behind them. The exam asks you to match a gene or inheritance pattern to a cardiovascular finding and to explain the mechanism.

notes.h: Genetic principles seen in heart disease
points: Most single-gene cardiovascular disorders are autosomal dominant (familial hypercholesterolemia, HCM, Marfan, most long QT).
Variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance are common, so relatives with the same variant can look very different.
Locus heterogeneity: one disease, many genes (familial hypercholesterolemia from LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9; long QT from many channel genes).
Pleiotropy: one gene, many organs (fibrillin-1 in Marfan affects aorta, eye, and skeleton).
Gene dosage matters: familial hypercholesterolemia homozygotes are far more severe than heterozygotes.
Mitochondrial DNA disorders can cause cardiomyopathy and conduction block (for example Kearns-Sayre syndrome); heteroplasmy explains variable severity.
Usually a mutation in the LDL receptor gene; APOB and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants cause the same picture.
Fewer working receptors means less LDL and IDL clearance, so more IDL becomes LDL.
Less cholesterol inside liver cells also takes the brake off cholesterol synthesis.
Heterozygotes have about two to three times normal plasma cholesterol; homozygotes about five to six times, often with MI before age 20.
Signs: tendon xanthomas (often Achilles), xanthelasma, early corneal arcus, premature coronary disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: sarcomere protein genes, most often MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C).
HCM shows myocyte disarray, asymmetric septal thickening, diastolic dysfunction, and a risk of sudden death in young athletes.
Congenital long QT comes from potassium channel loss (KCNQ1, KCNH2) or sodium channel gain (SCN5A), which delays repolarization and invites torsades de pointes.
Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is autosomal recessive long QT with sensorineural deafness; Romano-Ward syndrome is autosomal dominant without deafness.
Brugada syndrome: loss of function in SCN5A, ST elevation in V1 to V3 with a pseudo-right bundle branch block pattern, and sudden death risk.
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (dystrophin, X-linked) cause dilated cardiomyopathy; Friedreich ataxia (frataxin, GAA repeat) causes HCM.
Marfan syndrome: FBN1 (fibrillin-1) on chromosome 15; faulty microfibrils weaken elastic tissue and increase TGF-beta signaling.
Marfan cardiovascular findings: aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1 or TGFBR2): aggressive aortic aneurysms, arterial tortuosity, bifid uvula, widely spaced eyes.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1, type III collagen): arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.

notes.h: Gene expression and the cell cycle in the heart
points: Adult cardiomyocytes have largely left the cell cycle and renew very slowly, so dead myocardium is replaced by scar.
Under pressure or volume load, cardiomyocytes grow larger (hypertrophy) instead of dividing.
Hypertrophy reactivates fetal genes such as ANP, BNP, and beta-myosin heavy chain.
SREBP senses cell sterol levels and turns up LDL receptor and HMG-CoA reductase genes when cholesterol is low.
Smooth muscle cells in the intima proliferate in response to growth factors such as PDGF in atherosclerosis.

tricks.label: CATCH-22
tricks.text: 22q11.2 deletion: Cleft palate, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cardiac defects (conotruncal), Hypocalcemia from parathyroid aplasia, on chromosome 22.

tricks.label: Lens goes up in Marfan, down in homocystinuria
tricks.text: Both can look tall and thin with a dislocated lens. Marfan lenses usually shift up and out; homocystinuria lenses shift down and in, and homocystinuria adds clots.

tricks.label: Receptor down, LDL up
tricks.text: In familial hypercholesterolemia, picture the liver with half its LDL receptors. LDL piles up in plasma, and the cell, sensing too little cholesterol inside, keeps making more.

highYield: Familial hypercholesterolemia is autosomal dominant; homozygotes can have MI before age 20.
MYH7 and MYBPC3 are the most common HCM genes; inheritance is autosomal dominant.
Marfan syndrome is caused by FBN1 mutations; aortic dissection is the main cause of death.
Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome: long QT plus sensorineural deafness, autosomal recessive.
Down syndrome is most linked to atrioventricular septal defects.
Turner syndrome is linked to bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation.
Williams syndrome causes supravalvular aortic stenosis through elastin gene loss.
Hypertrophied myocytes switch back on fetal genes such as ANP, BNP, and beta-myosin heavy chain.
pitfalls: Marfan (FBN1) and Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1 or TGFBR2) both cause aortic aneurysm; Loeys-Dietz adds bifid uvula, widely spaced eyes, and arterial tortuosity.
Long QT from KCNQ1 and KCNH2 is a loss of potassium current, while SCN5A long QT is a gain of sodium current; Brugada is a loss of SCN5A function.
Cardiomyocytes respond to load by hypertrophy, while vascular smooth muscle cells can still proliferate.
Gain-of-function PCSK9 raises LDL; loss-of-function PCSK9 lowers it, because PCSK9 sends LDL receptors to be degraded.
